title: When Difficult Math Feels Easy
author: Samantha Lippert
summary: Samantha Lippert, a third-grade co-taught special education teacher, argues that explicit instruction is the pathway to conceptual understanding rather than its opposite. She shows what she means by walking through eight days of atomizing rounding to the nearest ten and hundred. Day 1 teaches no rounding at all and only has students identify the benchmark values around a number, and Day 2 adds the number line and the midpoint. The rounding rule is later derived from the visual model instead of being handed over as a trick, and she deliberately teaches hundreds before tens so that the structural change is mastered first. Every problem uses the same questioning sequence, which reduces extraneous load and makes misconceptions easy to locate. Mixed practice comes only on Day 8, after each component has been taught and practiced.
points: Atomizing means breaking a skill into every micro-component and teaching each explicitly before combining them, which protects limited working memory.
Spending a full day on identifying benchmark values makes the later idea of rounding feel like a natural conclusion rather than a new procedure.
Deriving the rounding rule from a number line gives the rule meaning, so students can explain why a number rounds up or down.
Reversing the usual order and teaching hundreds before tens lets students master the larger structural change first.
Scaffolds for struggling students reduce the problem back to a component rather than lowering the mathematical demand.
quotes: I started atomizing my math lessons—breaking a target skill down into every single micro-component a student needs before asking them to execute the larger task.
Explicit instruction isn’t the opposite of conceptual understanding. It is the pathway to it.
This mattered because I didn’t spend Day 1 of rounding reteaching place value. The prerequisite knowledge was secure, which freed up working memory for the new learning targets.

We spent an entire day on what standard curricula often reduce to a 30-second procedural step, “Find the two numbers it’s between”. But because we isolated this component, students understood why those benchmarks existed within our base-ten system.
This was the moment when the familiar “rounding rule” could finally make sense. But in this instructional sequence, the rule was derived from the visual model, not taught as a standalone trick.
Many commercial curricula teach rounding to the nearest ten before hundreds. In my classroom, we deliberately reverse that order.
The point of atomizing isn’t to make the mathematics less rigorous. It is to reduce the number of new things students must process simultaneously.
The scaffold allowed them to access the concept without lowering the mathematical demand.
